query: FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy alloys are promising bond-coat candidates because of their mechanical properties and elevated-temperature oxidation resistance. Earlier HVAF-M3 work identified 15–45 μm feedstock as optimal for high-quality coatings, but applying the same composition and size range with the HVAF-i7 torch yielded acceptable coating quality yet inadequate thickness. Separate studies of conventional MCrAlY bond coats using the M3 system reported a slight gain in deposition efficiency at higher particle velocity and nozzle-specific best spray distances of 300 and 350 mm. The design target is a sufficiently thick, adherent bond coat that retains coating integrity, minimal as-sprayed oxidation, and durability during high-temperature thermal-barrier service, including deposition within internal diameters as small as 120 mm. What single intervention could overcome the thickness limitation? State the hypothesized intervention and mechanism, predict the outcome relative to the 15–45 μm-feedstock baseline, define the deposition and service conditions under which it should remain effective, identify supporting evidence from the cited prior studies, and propose a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Optimizing the spray distance to around 300–350 mm on the HVAF‐i7 system—thus effectively increasing the particle velocity at impact—will overcome the thickness limitation encountered with the 15–45 μm feedstock while maintaining minimal as-sprayed oxidation and coating integrity.
generation.material_initial_state: FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy alloy powder with a 15–45 μm size distribution, as previously shown to yield high-quality but thin coatings on the HVAF-i7 system.
generation.intervention: Adjust the HVAF-i7 deposition parameters by increasing the stand-off (spray) distance to about 300–350 mm to boost the in-flight velocity of the particles.
generation.conditions: Deposition in environments consistent with high-temperature oxidation resistance and within internal diameters as small as 120 mm, similar to operational conditions for bond coats in thermal-barrier systems.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced kinetic energy of the in-flight particles, which improves splat formation and deposition efficiency.
generation.mechanism: Increasing the spray distance allows the particles more time to accelerate and reach a higher velocity before impact. This higher momentum improves adhesion and packing density on the substrate, leading to a thicker, more robust coating. It also minimizes excessive in-flight oxidation by reducing the residence time over the substrate, thus preserving the desired microstructure.
generation.predicted_outcome: A significantly thicker, adherent bond coat with comparable oxidation levels and microstructural integrity relative to the baseline established with the HVAF-M3 process but adapted for the HVAF-i7 system.
generation.baseline: Deposition using the HVAF-i7 torch at the original spray distance with 15–45 μm feedstock, which produces acceptable coating quality but insufficient thickness.
generation.boundary: The optimized spray distance and increased particle velocity should be effective as long as processing is performed within the geometric constraints (e.g., internal diameters down to 120 mm) and the high-temperature environment does not alter the improved kinetic profile significantly; deviations may occur if the enhanced distance introduces additional challenges in particle heating or substrate access.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of the thickness gain and any potential trade-offs in coating microstructure or residual oxidation levels are uncertain without empirical validation; additional studies may be required to fine-tune the exact spray distance and particle acceleration parameters specific to the HVAF-i7 configuration.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct comparative deposition experiments using the HVAF-i7 torch with the standard spray distance versus an optimized spray distance of 300–350 mm, keeping the feedstock (15–45 μm) and all other parameters constant. Evaluate the resultant coating thickness, adhesion, microstructure, and oxidation level.
measurements: Coating thickness (via cross-sectional microscopy and profilometry)
Microstructural analysis (using SEM and XRD to assess phase composition and oxidation)
Hardness and wear resistance (via microhardness testing and tribological evaluation)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the optimized spray distance does not produce a statistically significant increase in coating thickness without detrimental changes in adhesion, microstructural integrity, or oxidation levels compared to the baseline HVAF-i7 deposition, the hypothesis would be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: One of the most promising applications of AlCoCrFeNi HEA is the fabrication of protective coatings [,]. HEA-based coatings, deposited on medium-carbon steel substrates, can considerably enhance the material performances, extend service life, and reduce product costs [,,]. Thick coatings with low porosity and a high level of adhesion can be produced via the high velocity fuel spraying (HVOF) technique [,]. HVOF is a combustion spray process in which a hydrocarbon fuel (kerosene, methane, propane, etc.) is ignited, mixing with oxygen to accelerate feedstock powder towards the substrate [,]. Depending on the particle’s size and location in the high-temperature flow, the particles undergo various transformations, such as melting, softening, spheroidization, precipitation, and surface or total oxidation, similar to those observed with the atmospheric plasma spraying (APS) method []. Lower particle temperatures than those achieved in plasma spraying and higher particle speeds result in lower in-flight particle oxidation and better coating densities.
